title: RIS Christie (Aug 1996 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Ruling
subject: TCC trial decision assessing whether spatial membrane panel research qualified as SR&ED under Regulation 2900.
outcome: Appeal dismissed by TCC for lack of repeatable test data (later reversed by FCA in 1998 CanLII 8876).
summary: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen is a key Canadian SR&ED case. In 1996, the Tax Court of Canada denied the taxpayer's research deduction, allowance and investment tax credit for lacking documented experimental repeatability. In 1998, the Federal Court of Appeal reversed, holding that documentary proof is not mandatory once testing and a technological advancement are established.
metaDescription: Explore the August 1996 Tax Court of Canada decision for RIS Christie and how it shaped Canadian SR&ED tax credit litigation.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The litigation in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen—spanning the trial judgment of the Tax Court of Canada handed down on August 28, 1996 (reported at 97 DTC 99, [1996] 3 C.T.C. 2827) and its subsequent appellate reversal by the Federal Court of Appeal on December 21, 1998 (Docket A-710-96, reported at 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 1998 CanLII 8876)—stands as one of the foundational pillars of Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax jurisprudence. The case addresses a recurring point of friction in Canadian tax law: whether a taxpayer whose experimental development is accepted, on the evidence, to have resolved an engineering uncertainty and yielded a patented technological advancement can nevertheless be disqualified from SR&ED tax incentives due to deficient contemporaneous documentation that fails to guarantee the third-party "repeatability" of the underlying tests.
Factual Matrix and Commercial Genesis

In 1982, Leon Slonimsky (identified as "Leonid" Slonimsky in the Federal Court of Appeal's reasons), a professional engineer, and Daniel D. Dorcich, a businessman—both principals of Plyform Construction Company Limited ("PCCL")—conceived of a concrete forming medium for cast-in-situ (poured-in-place) concrete construction, described in the proposal to investors as "a Closed body-type Spatial Membrane with integral Heating Element and Thermal Insulation" and designated as a "spatial membrane panel". The objective of the spatial membrane panel was to decrease costs and increase the quality of insulation in the formation of concrete panels for use by the residential and non-residential construction industry; as described by Dorcich, the uncertainty was whether an ultra-light or very lightweight composite structure, unlike anything available in the existing market, could technically be developed and produced at competitive market prices.

In November 1982, PCCL (Slonimsky and Dorcich) prepared a research and development proposal for distribution to interested investors; it reached Brian E. Turner of Williams & Turner Consultants Inc. ("Consultants"), a manager of scientific research and development projects, who approached RIS-Christie Ltd. Pursuant to an agreement executed as of December 1, 1982 between Consultants and a newly incorporated Ontario numbered corporation, 541185 Ontario Inc. (referred to in the judicial record as "541185"), 541185 undertook to perform the requisite research and development of the spatial membrane panel and Consultants undertook to provide the necessary funds. The corporate appellant, RIS-Christie Ltd., agreed to invest in the project; the Tax Court records that $230,000 was received by 541185 under this arrangement in the 1983 taxation year (the Federal Court of Appeal summarized this as a $230,000 investment made in December 1982 through a numbered company), while Slonimsky and Dorcich agreed to execute the technical research and experimental development activities.

The technical execution of the project proceeded across three distinct multi-year phases that bridged initial theoretical modelling and final intellectual property protection. Phase I took place throughout the 1983 taxation year—beginning, according to Dorcich, upon receipt of the first instalment of funds in March 1983—focusing on data collection and review of existing concrete forming systems and patents, detailed conceptual drawings and analysis, and experiments to determine the optimum dimensions and materials of the panel, which produced a working prototype of the spatial membrane panel by the end of calendar year 1983 with a view to testing it under field conditions in 1984. Phases II and III, for which further funding was received in April 1984, continued across the 1984 and 1985 taxation years, encompassing iterative refinement, material optimization, and structural testing of the panel system. This multi-year experimental progression ultimately culminated in the filing of a Canadian patent application on January 31, 1986, which matured into a Canadian patent granted on April 30, 1991 to 589576 Ontario Inc., a successor corporation to 541185.
The Taxpayer's Statutory Claim and the Minister's Challenge

In calculating its income for the taxation year ended December 31, 1982, RIS-Christie Ltd. claimed three interlocking statutory tax incentives under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), as amended (the "Act" or "ITA") in respect of its investment in the concrete forming medium project (the Federal Court of Appeal later noted that it was common ground that the research expenditures properly related to the 1983 taxation year rather than the 1982 taxation year as originally claimed). First, the taxpayer claimed a deduction of $160,000 for scientific research expenditures pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act. Second, it claimed an additional research allowance of $80,000—the 50% incremental SR&ED deduction regime applicable to corporate taxpayers during that statutory period—pursuant to subsection 37.1(1) and paragraph 37.1(5)(e) of the Act. Third, the corporation claimed an investment tax credit (ITC) of $40,000 pursuant to subsection 127(9) of the Act.

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through Revenue Canada (now the Canada Revenue Agency, or "CRA"), assessed RIS-Christie Ltd.'s 1982 taxation year and disallowed the paragraph 37(1)(a) SR&ED deduction, the subsection 37.1(1) research allowance, and the subsection 127(9) ITC in their entirety, and, as a consequence, reassessed its 1983 taxation year by reducing the small business deduction claimed under section 125 of the Act. The Minister's challenge rested on the assertion that the development activities conducted on the spatial membrane panel did not constitute "scientific research" (now uniformly termed "scientific research and experimental development") within the meaning of section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"); the parties agreed that, if scientific research was in fact conducted, the expenses were prescribed expenditures within the meaning of Regulations 2901 and 2902 and the research was sufficiently related to the appellant's business. Specifically, the Crown contended that scientific investigation within the meaning of Regulation 2900 involves repeatable steps which are clearly noted, and that the taxpayer had failed to produce documentation of the experiments demonstrating recorded parameters capable of independent verification and replication.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

During the taxation years in dispute, the substantive definition of eligible R&D was housed in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations, which applied to Part XXIX of the Regulations and paragraphs 37(7)(b) and 37.1(5)(e) of the Act. In subsequent legislative consolidations, Parliament migrated this exact definition from Regulation 2900(1) directly into subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act without material alteration to its core architecture. As reproduced by the Court, subsection 2900(1) defined "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory scheme divided qualifying work into three primary streams: basic research under paragraph 2900(1)(a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research under paragraph 2900(1)(b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and development under paragraph 2900(1)(c) (now termed "experimental development" under paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Act), defined as the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes. Under the consolidated subsection 248(1) regime, this core definition is supplemented by paragraph 248(1)(d), which includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada, while paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) expressly exclude routine testing, quality control, commercial production, style changes, and market research.

In interpreting this statutory text alongside Revenue Canada's administrative guidance in Information Circular IC 86-4R3 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development), Canadian jurisprudence crystallized a five-part analytical framework first articulated by Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.)—a decision rendered after the Tax Court's 1996 RIS-Christie judgment, which therefore did not apply it and relied instead on Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (T.C.C.)—to which the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie referred at paragraph 10 as a comprehensive analysis of the meaning of "scientific research" without itself restating the test, and which was subsequently endorsed in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (at paragraph 6), and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (at paragraph 7). Under this governing five-question test, the Court evaluates: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed.
The Judicial Holdings: Tax Court Disqualification vs. Appellate Reversal

The procedural history of RIS-Christie presents a sharp dichotomy between the trial decision in the Tax Court of Canada and the final disposition in the Federal Court of Appeal. Following the trial (heard on July 4 and 5, 1994 and June 8 and 9, 1995) leading to the August 28, 1996 decision (97 DTC 99), the Tax Court Judge (Sarchuk T.C.J.) stated that there was "some evidence" in the taxpayer's favour on the core technical activities: some evidence that an engineering uncertainty existed, that a hypothesis was formulated, and that by testing models and by observation of the results 541185 resolved the problem and created a practical product which embodied a technological advance; he also accepted that Dorcich's testimony confirmed that investigation and experimentation to develop a product was conducted in the taxation years in issue and that a new product was created, and the Federal Court of Appeal later read these statements, in context, as findings of fact. Notwithstanding these statements, the Tax Court Judge dismissed the taxpayer's appeal for the 1983 taxation year on the SR&ED issue (the appeal for the 1982 taxation year was allowed solely on a separate reserve issue pursuant to a Partial Consent to Judgment). Relying on his earlier decision in Sass Manufacturing and on the evidence of the Crown's expert witness, Dr. A. Ghani Razaqpur, which he expressly accepted, the trial judge held that "repeatability" is an essential element of scientific research flowing from the requirement of a "systematic investigation" under Regulation 2900. Because there were "substantial shortcomings" in the direct evidence adduced on behalf of RIS-Christie Ltd. on repeatability, and concluding that repeatability had been established would have required speculation rather than inference from proven facts, the Tax Court dismissed the appeal, leaving the disallowance of the SR&ED deduction, research allowance, and ITC in place.

Upon further appeal by the taxpayer in Docket A-710-96, decided on December 21, 1998 (99 DTC 5087), the Federal Court of Appeal—in unanimous reasons delivered by Justice Robertson and concurred in by Justices Strayer and Sexton—allowed the taxpayer's appeal with costs in both the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court, set aside the Tax Court judgment, and allowed the appeal from the Minister's assessments, thereby restoring the paragraph 37(1)(a) SR&ED deduction, the subsection 37.1(1) research allowance, and the subsection 127(9) ITC. The Federal Court of Appeal held that, while adducing documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests is the only "sure-fire" way to establish that research was systematic, both documentary and viva voce evidence are admissible, and the Income Tax Act does not impose an absolute requirement that SR&ED be proven exclusively by documentary evidence. Once the Tax Court Judge found that testing had been undertaken and that the research efforts constituted a technological advancement in the construction industry, a rebuttable inference arose that the testing was carried out in accordance with Regulation 2900, and the trial judge erred by imposing an additional evidentiary burden requiring documentary proof of the repeatability of testing data.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Although RIS-Christie Ltd. ultimately secured an appellate reversal sixteen years after its initial 1982 investment, the underlying reassessment dispute—and the taxpayer's complete defeat at the Tax Court of Canada in August 1996—stemmed from four severe legal, evidentiary, contractual, and operational deficiencies. In contemporary Canadian tax practice, where Tax Court judges routinely refuse to make favourable factual findings of systematic experimentation in the absence of contemporaneous records, these exact deficiencies remain fatal to SR&ED claims.
2.1 The "Repeatability" Criterion and Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies

The primary catalyst for the disallowance in RIS-Christie was the taxpayer's inability to produce detailed, contemporaneous experimental logs recording the exact parameters, variables, measurements, and analytical iterations of the 1983 spatial membrane panel tests. At the Tax Court of Canada, the Crown argued that the statutory phrase "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" in subsection 2900(1) inherently requires that experiments be documented with sufficient quantitative precision that an independent practitioner can reproduce the test conditions.

Counsel for the Crown submitted that the definition of scientific research cannot be met unless it is possible to provide "a recorded basis upon which others can perform the same experiments and are able to verify or disprove the hypothesis by setting up the exact same test parameters", and that scientific investigation within Regulation 2900 involves "repeatable steps which are clearly noted". The Tax Court Judge, relying on his statement in Sass Manufacturing that systematic investigation would include repeatable experiments in which the steps, the various changes made and the results are carefully noted, treated repeatability as a requisite element of scientific research flowing from the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation"; the Federal Court of Appeal characterized this as the Tax Court Judge accepting the Minister's position. When examining the fragmentary records adduced by RIS-Christie Ltd. at trial, the Tax Court Judge identified "substantial shortcomings" in the direct evidence on repeatability: while the evidence showed that a prototype was built and eventually patented, there was very little evidence that essential information—the type, size and number of specimens, the test set-up, the test methodology, the instrumentation and data acquisition system, the test data collected, the analysis and interpretation of that data, and the correlation of test data to the original hypothesis—had been recorded for the work executed in 1983.

In correcting the trial judge's legal error, Justice Robertson of the Federal Court of Appeal articulated a nuanced evidentiary doctrine in paragraphs 14 through 16 of the appellate judgment that continues to govern CRA compliance reviews today. The Court first affirmed that in addition to developing new products or processes, scientific research connotes the existence of controlled experiments involving the testing of models or prototypes, and that taxpayers must demonstrate not only that tests were performed but that they were conducted in a systematic fashion. Second, the Court emphasized that, although both documentary and viva voce evidence are admissible, the only "sure-fire" way of demonstrating that scientific research was undertaken in a systematic fashion is to adduce documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests. Third, however, the Court distinguished between what constitutes SR&ED in law and how SR&ED is proven in court. Repeatability is not an independent statutory condition precedent that negates the validity of all other admissible evidence; rather, where a taxpayer has a plausible explanation for the absence of documentary evidence (for example, research notes accidentally destroyed), or where it is established that the research led to a technological advancement, the court may infer on a balance of probabilities, having regard to the totality of the evidence, that systematic research was conducted.

Because the trial judge in RIS-Christie had, in the Federal Court of Appeal's reading, already found that testing had been undertaken and that the research efforts of Slonimsky and his assistant constituted a technological advancement—findings that raised a rebuttable inference that the testing was carried out in accordance with Regulation 2900—elevating the missing repeatability documentation into an additional evidentiary burden was unwarranted in the circumstances. Nevertheless, as subsequent Tax Court decisions such as National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 67) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 246; aff'd 2021 FCA 88) demonstrate, when a modern taxpayer lacks contemporaneous test records, trial judges simply decline to find that systematic testing occurred in the first place, thereby dismissing the appeal on factual findings that cannot be overturned by the Federal Court of Appeal.
2.2 Witness Unavailability, Key-Person Risk, and the Unproduced "Georgetown Documents"

The documentary deficit in RIS-Christie was compounded by a severe breakdown in the taxpayer's evidentiary chain of custody between the 1983 taxation year and the August 1996 Tax Court trial. Leon Slonimsky (identified as "Leonid" in the Federal Court of Appeal's reasons), the professional engineer whose domain was the engineering aspect of the project and who, together with another engineer aided by a generalist, was responsible for the actual design and the engineering calculations for each part and component of the panel, died prior to the Tax Court trial. Consequently, the single witness capable of providing direct, first-hand viva voce technical testimony explaining the mathematical analysis, structural mechanics, and experimental protocol—and, as Dorcich conceded, the only person who could have repeated the experiments—was permanently unavailable to the Court. Furthermore, Daniel Dorcich, the businessman who collaborated with Slonimsky on the project, was in poor health at the time of the hearing and could not attend in Court; by agreement, his evidence was tendered by way of an affidavit and cross-examination upon that affidavit. While Dorcich's testimony confirmed at a general level that investigation and experimentation were conducted during the taxation years in issue and that a new product was created, a businessman's affidavit evidence and cross-examination could not reconstruct the granular engineering telemetry of the 1983 structural tests.

This testimonial vulnerability was exacerbated by the unexplained non-production of what the judicial record refers to as the "Georgetown documents". Evidence at trial—given by the appellant's expert, Edward L. Littlejohn—revealed that he had reviewed hundreds of pages of documents containing sketches, drawings, conclusions and calculations collected by Slonimsky, stored in five or six large boxes in a barn at the late Mr. Slonimsky's former residence in Georgetown, Ontario. For reasons that remained unexplained at trial (no explanation for their absence was proffered), these Georgetown documents were never produced in evidence before the Tax Court of Canada. Under Canadian tax litigation principles, the legal onus rests squarely on the taxpayer to demolish the Minister's assumptions of fact, and a party's failure to produce material documents within its power or control routinely invites an adverse inference that the unproduced records would not have supported the claim. In RIS-Christie, the Tax Court Judge expressly stated that he drew no adverse inference from the appellant's failure to produce the documents viewed at Georgetown; however, he described Littlejohn's failure to produce or properly document that material as "unpardonable," gave no weight to Littlejohn's conclusions, and held that, although Littlejohn testified that some Georgetown documents initialled and dated by Slonimsky "reflected work done and tests carried out" (a statement the Federal Court of Appeal treated as a finding of the trial judge), nothing established on a balance of probabilities the existence of recorded information capable of making the experiments or tests repeatable. From a corporate tax governance perspective, allowing core SR&ED test records to remain sequestered at a contractor's private residence without corporate archiving or duplicate custody represents a critical compliance failure.
2.3 Contractual and Governance Deficiencies in Financed / Third-Party R&D Structures

A third structural failure illuminated by RIS-Christie involves the contractual governance of third-party or investor-financed R&D under section 37 of the Income Tax Act. RIS-Christie Ltd. did not perform the physical concrete experimentation in-house with its own salaried engineering workforce; instead, it agreed to invest in the project through Consultants, which, under the December 1, 1982 agreement with 541185 Ontario Inc., undertook to provide the necessary funds, while 541185 (with Slonimsky and Dorcich carrying out the work) undertook to perform the research and development; the Tax Court records that $230,000 was received by 541185 in the 1983 taxation year.

While the Income Tax Act permits a taxpayer to claim eligible expenditures for SR&ED carried on "by or on behalf of the taxpayer" under section 37 and subsection 248(1), the legal burden of substantiating that the underlying physical activities satisfy Regulation 2900 (the criteria later synthesized in Northwest Hydraulic) falls entirely upon the claiming taxpayer. The December 1, 1982 contractual arrangement—which, as the Tax Court noted, contained no information regarding the nature of the research being carried on—lacked protective technical compliance governance in three vital respects. First, the R&D agreement failed to enforce mandatory periodic transfer or escrow of raw experimental logs, structural calculations, and prototype test data from the R&D performers (541185 Ontario Inc. and Slonimsky) to the funding parties (Consultants and, ultimately, RIS-Christie Ltd.) as a condition precedent to funding disbursements. Second, the project governance tracked high-level commercial outputs—namely, the delivery of a working prototype at the end of Phase I in 1983 and the eventual filing of a Canadian patent application in January 1986—rather than tracking the statutory elements of Regulation 2900(1), such as the formal articulation of technological uncertainty, the formulation of specific hypotheses, systematic testing protocols, and quantitative analysis of results. Third, the taxpayer's counsel submitted that the granting of patent protection was relevant and persuasive evidence that scientific research occurred. The Tax Court held, however, that while the patent was some evidence that a new or improved product was created, it was not dispositive of whether scientific research within the meaning of Regulation 2900 had been conducted in the taxation years in issue, since a patent establishes an invention—a "new and useful" art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter under the Patent Act—whereas Regulation 2900 and subsection 248(1) require proof of a systematic investigation conducted during the specific taxation year claimed. An invention achieved through routine engineering adaptation or undocumented trial-and-error may be patentable yet wholly ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives.
2.4 Expert Witness Overreach vs. Judicial Interpretation of Statutory Criteria

The fourth major legal pitfall in RIS-Christie arose from the improper role accorded to expert witness testimony during the August 1996 Tax Court trial. Both the taxpayer's expert and the Crown's expert agreed on a general baseline proposition that "scientific research and development is considered to be the application of scientific and engineering principles to the resolution of a scientific or technical problem". However, the Crown's expert witness, Dr. Razaqpur, went further by articulating a five-step academic model of scientific research—formulating the problem, constructing the model, testing the model, deriving a solution from the model, and testing and implementing the solution—and testifying that documented "repeatability" is an indispensable attribute of scientific research.

The Tax Court Judge accepted Dr. Razaqpur's evidence and relied heavily on it, together with his own earlier decision in Sass Manufacturing, in treating repeatability as an essential element of scientific research under Regulation 2900, although he acknowledged that a less rigorous standard than that espoused by scientists involved in pure or applied research might be appropriate for the development of new technology. On appeal, Justice Robertson dismantled this approach in paragraph 12 of the Federal Court of Appeal decision, establishing a binding evidentiary rule cited across decades of subsequent Canadian SR&ED litigation, including Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 246 (at paragraph 24). Justice Robertson held that what constitutes "scientific research" for the purposes of the Income Tax Act is either a question of law or a question of mixed law and fact to be determined exclusively by the Tax Court of Canada, not by expert witnesses. An expert witness cannot usurp the judicial function by defining the statutory threshold of subsection 248(1) or Regulation 2900. Instead, "at the end of the day, the expert's role is limited to providing the court with a set of prescription glasses through which technical information may be viewed". It remains the sole prerogative of the trial judge to prefer one technical perspective over another and to evaluate the factual evidence against the legal standard enacted by Parliament.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential SR&ED requirement examined in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen against the taxpayer's evidentiary posture, the Tax Court of Canada's August 1996 disqualification standard, and the Federal Court of Appeal's corrective legal standard.

headers: Taxpayer's Evidentiary Posture & Operational Failure in RIS-Christie
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof (August 1996 Ruling, 97 DTC 99)
Federal Court of Appeal Corrective Standard & Modern CRA Practice (99 DTC 5087)

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1) (now ITA s. 248(1)); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); IC 86-4R3.

Conceived a novel "spatial membrane panel" for cast-in-situ concrete construction to reduce costs and increase insulation quality; Dorcich outlined the engineering uncertainty "quite adequately," but Dr. Razaqpur characterized the documented drawings and calculations as a routine engineering exercise within the grasp of any competent structural engineer.

Some Evidence: The Tax Court Judge stated that there was "some evidence" that an engineering uncertainty existed; he made no express finding that the uncertainty could not be resolved by routine engineering.

Affirmed: Research must involve an element of creativity rather than the mere application of routine engineering principles (FCA para. 13); the FCA read the trial judge's "some evidence" statements, in context, as findings of fact (para. 9).
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1) (now ITA s. 248(1)); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2).

PCCL prepared an R&D proposal in November 1982 outlining the basic requirements for a new concrete forming medium (criticized in a January 18, 1983 engineering review as requiring a much more comprehensive feasibility study), but failed to preserve iterative written hypothesis logs as testing progressed in 1983.
Some Evidence: The trial judge stated there was some evidence that a hypothesis was formulated, but noted that Dorcich could not describe, beyond the most general terms, the hypotheses being tested.

Not Separately Restated by the FCA: The five-stage process (observation, objective, articulation of uncertainty, hypothesis formulation, methodical testing) derives from Northwest Hydraulic, to which the FCA referred at para. 10, and is provable through documentary or credible testimonial evidence.
3. Accordance with the Scientific Method ("Systematic Investigation")
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1) (now ITA s. 248(1)); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3).

Built and tested physical models in Phase I (1983) and Phases II–III (1984–1985); lead engineer Slonimsky died prior to trial; businessman Dorcich attested to model testing via affidavit and cross-examination on it, describing early shop tests as done "to get the feel of the matter," with results not necessarily recorded and tested parts discarded.

Disqualified on Law/Evidence: Despite noting some evidence that models were tested and results observed, the TCC held that repeatability—repeatable experiments in which the steps, changes and results are carefully noted (Sass Manufacturing)—is an essential element of a systematic investigation, and that concluding it was established would require speculation.

Reversed TCC Error of Law: Scientific research connotes controlled experiments involving the testing of models or prototypes, but once the trial judge found that testing had been undertaken and a technological advance achieved, a rebuttable inference arose that the testing accorded with Regulation 2900, and lack of documented repeatability could not negate eligibility.
4. Technological Advancement
Income Tax Regulations s. 2900(1)(c) (now ITA s. 248(1)(c)); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4).
Produced a working prototype by year-end 1983; filed Canadian patent application on January 31, 1986; Canadian patent granted to successor corporation 589576 Ontario Inc. on April 30, 1991.

Some Evidence: The Tax Court Judge stated there was some evidence that a practical product embodying a technological advance was created; the patent was some evidence of a new or improved product but not dispositive.

Affirmed and Expanded: The FCA treated the technological advance in the construction industry as established and held that it permits an inference that systematic research was conducted (paras. 15–16); it also held that there is no statutory requirement that eligible research actually culminate in a technological advancement (para. 13).
5. Contemporaneous Documentation & Repeatability of Test Data
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); ITA s. 230(1) (Books and Records); CRA Claim Review Manual (CRM) s. 5.12.1.

Records that Littlejohn said he reviewed in boxes in a barn at Slonimsky's former residence in Georgetown were never produced at trial; the direct evidence adduced had "substantial shortcomings" on repeatability, with very little evidence that specimens, test set-up, methodology, instrumentation, test data and analysis were recorded.

Fatal Disqualification: Treated repeatability as an essential element: on the evidence, concluding that it had been established would have required speculation rather than inference from proven facts, so the claim failed.

Evidentiary vs. Substantive Distinction: Detailed contemporaneous records revealing the logical progression between tests are the only "sure-fire" way to prove systematic SR&ED, but documentary proof is not mandatory where there is a plausible explanation for its absence or where a technological advancement is established (paras. 14–16).
6. Third-Party R&D Governance & Chain of Custody
ITA s. 37(1)(a), s. 37.1(1), s. 127(9); Income Tax Regulations s. 2900–2902.

RIS-Christie Ltd. invested through Consultants, which funded 541185 Ontario Inc. under a Dec. 1, 1982 agreement ($230,000 received by 541185 in 1983), but failed to secure custodial control over Slonimsky's engineering logs or mitigate key-person mortality risk.

No Adverse Inference Drawn, But Claim Denied: Trial judge expressly drew no adverse inference from the non-production of the Georgetown documents, but gave no weight to Littlejohn's conclusions based on them and found no proof of recorded information capable of making the tests repeatable.

High Litigation Risk Warning: While RIS-Christie survived on appeal due to the trial judge's generous factual findings, modern TCC jurisprudence (Jentel, Kam-Press, National R&D) routinely dismisses claims where records are missing.
7. Role of Expert Witness Testimony
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure); Common Law Evidence Rules.
Crown expert (Dr. Razaqpur) testified that a five-step process and documented "repeatability" are essential attributes of scientific research.

Relied Heavily on Expert Evidence: Accepted Dr. Razaqpur's evidence and, together with Sass Manufacturing, treated repeatability as essential under Regulation 2900, while acknowledging that a less rigorous standard might be appropriate for new technology development.

Strictly Circumscribed ("Prescription Glasses" Rule): What constitutes SR&ED under the ITA is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the Judge alone; experts only provide "prescription glasses" to view technical facts.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial lessons of RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen into actionable tax and engineering compliance protocols, the following two applied Canadian industry case studies examine realistic corporate R&D projects confronting the exact legal, contractual, and evidentiary traps identified in the ruling. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial architecture designed to satisfy subsection 248(1), section 37, and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, and Chapter 5 of the CRA's Claim Review Manual (CRM) for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs).
Case Study 1: Structural & Civil Materials Engineering — Subcontracted Development of a Load-Bearing Insulating Stay-in-Place Concrete Formwork System
Scenario & Alignment with RIS-Christie Pitfalls

Laurentian Structural Systems Inc. ("Laurentian"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Mississauga, Ontario, specializes in engineered building envelope systems. In its 2025 taxation year, Laurentian commits $650,000 to develop a next-generation, stay-in-place composite polymer-cementitious spatial forming panel for high-rise cast-in-situ concrete shear walls, directly paralleling the civil engineering domain in RIS-Christie. The technical objective is to achieve a 35% reduction in hydrostatic lateral form-pressure deflection during rapid winter pours while maintaining an integrated thermal resistance of R-28 without spalling or delamination at the concrete-membrane interface.

Laurentian contracts the core structural modelling and physical load-testing to an external specialist engineering firm, Vaughn Advanced Materials Inc. ("Vaughn Inc."), led by a semi-retired principal structural engineer, Dr. K. Petrov. Halfway through the 2025 taxation year, after constructing and testing twelve physical panel prototypes that culminate in a successful patent filing, Dr. Petrov suffers a debilitating medical emergency and relocates overseas, rendering him unavailable for CRA audit interviews or Tax Court testimony. All raw strain-gauge data, hydraulic load-cell logs, and failed prototype records remain on Dr. Petrov's local workstation and in physical notebooks stored at his private residence outside Toronto, which are subsequently misplaced. Laurentian possesses only the December 2024 R&D contract, quarterly progress invoices, CAD drawings of the final successful prototype, and the Canadian patent application. During a CRA SR&ED review, the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) issues an unfavourable draft review report citing RIS-Christie and Northwest Hydraulic, asserting that Laurentian has provided only indirect evidence of a final product without contemporaneous documentary proof of systematic hypothesis testing or experimental repeatability.
Step 1: Project Governance & Key-Person Custodial Architecture

To eliminate the "Georgetown documents" and witness-unavailability trap that crippled RIS-Christie Ltd. before the Tax Court of Canada, Laurentian must establish a centralized, cloud-synchronized SR&ED Technical Evidence Repository (STER) under Laurentian's direct corporate custody prior to project commencement. Rather than allowing field engineers or third-party contractors to retain experimental notebooks at off-site locations or private residences, corporate governance protocols must enforce automated weekly synchronization of all raw finite element analysis (FEA) models, laboratory bench sheets, hydraulic load-test telemetry, and environmental chamber logs directly into Laurentian's corporate server architecture.

Simultaneously, Laurentian must mitigate key-person testimonial risk by mandating dual-custodian technical oversight across every phase of the subcontracted project. Every experimental phase must pair an internal Laurentian professional engineer as Co-Investigator alongside the external lead engineer at Vaughn Inc. Both engineers must co-sign monthly structured technical progress logs recorded contemporaneously in the normal course of business. Under section 30 of the Canada Evidence Act (the business records exception to the hearsay rule) and Tax Court of Canada evidentiary practice, should the external lead investigator pass away or become medically incapacitated prior to audit or trial as occurred with Mr. Slonimsky and Mr. Dorcich in RIS-Christie, the internal Co-Investigator can take the witness stand to authenticate the contemporaneous business records and deliver direct, credible viva voce testimony explaining the experimental methodology.
Step 2: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation & Repeatability Protocols

To satisfy both the Tax Court of Canada's strict "repeatability" standard (97 DTC 99) and the Federal Court of Appeal's observation that documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between tests is the only "sure-fire" way of proving systematic SR&ED (99 DTC 5087, paragraphs 14–15), Laurentian must implement a standardized Experimental Repeatability & Parameter Log (ERPL) for every prototype iteration. Each ERPL entry must open with a formal Baseline Technological Uncertainty Statement satisfying Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic, documenting mathematically why standard American Concrete Institute (ACI) and CSA A23.1 concrete formwork equations cannot predict the viscoelastic creep and shear-bond interaction between the novel polymer-cementitious membrane and curing exothermic cast-in-situ concrete.

Prior to executing each physical concrete pour test, the engineering team must record a falsifiable engineering hypothesis satisfying Criterion 2 of Northwest Hydraulic. This written hypothesis must specify the mathematical relationship between controlled independent variables—such as glass-fibre internal truss angle θ, polymer resin cross-link density, concrete slump, pour velocity in m/h, and ambient curing temperature—and measured dependent structural parameters, specifically lateral deflection in mm, interfacial bond shear strength in MPa, and thermal conductivity λ-value. Crucially, to satisfy Criteria 3 and 5 regarding systematic investigation and repeatability, the ERPL for each of the twelve prototype tests must archive the exact boundary conditions, calibration certificates of the strain gauges, control sample parameters, raw quantitative time-series sensor outputs, and post-failure forensic analyses. This level of documentary granularity guarantees that any independent structural engineer reviewing the file—including a CRA RTA or a Crown expert witness—can replicate the exact test parameters and verify how each failed test informed the modification of the subsequent hypothesis.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring & R&D Performer Covenants

To remedy the defective December 1, 1982 agreement structure in RIS-Christie, Laurentian must redraft its Master R&D Subcontract Agreement with Vaughn Inc. to incorporate four interlocking Canadian tax compliance covenants. First, the contract must include a Statutory Scope and Subsection 248(1) Alignment Clause expressly stipulating that all contracted engineering and testing work is undertaken in Canada "on behalf of" Laurentian pursuant to subsection 248(1) and paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, while requiring line-item billing segregation between eligible experimental development activities under paragraph 248(1)(c), directly supporting engineering and testing under paragraph 248(1)(d), and excluded commercial production or routine quality control under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i).

Second, the agreement must establish Contemporaneous Documentation Delivery as a strict legal condition precedent to milestone payment disbursement. Rather than paying against generic commercial invoices or prototype delivery milestones, Laurentian must withhold 30% of each progressive tranche until Vaughn Inc. uploads the completed Experimental Repeatability & Parameter Logs, raw sensor CSV files, and failed test photographs into Laurentian's corporate repository and the internal Co-Investigator verifies their completeness under subsection 230(1) of the Act. Third, an Evidentiary Ownership and Anti-Sequestration Clause must vest immediate, unconditional legal title and physical custody of all working papers, lab notebooks, physical test coupons, and raw experimental data in Laurentian the moment they are generated, explicitly prohibiting off-site personal retention by contractor personnel. Fourth, an Audit Cooperation and Contemporaneous Affidavit Covenant must obligate Dr. Petrov and all participating subcontractor personnel to attend CRA RTA on-site interviews and to execute detailed, notarized statutory declarations at the close of each fiscal year summarizing the hypotheses tested, experimental parameters, and conclusions reached while their memory is intact, thereby insulating the taxpayer against witness mortality or infirmity during multi-year litigation.
Step 4: Systematic Experimentation Tracking & CRA Audit Defense Alignment

During the CRA review, Laurentian will avoid the fatal mistake of relying on its Canadian patent application or working prototype as self-proving evidence of SR&ED. Instead, Laurentian will present a unified Form T661 Technical Claim Dossier that maps every dollar of subcontracted paragraph 37(1)(a) expenditures and subsection 127(9) ITC claims directly to the chronological sequence of twelve hypothesis-test-analysis loops. Should the CRA retain an external structural engineering expert who attempts to impose an elevated academic threshold of scientific research beyond the text of subsection 248(1), Laurentian's tax litigation counsel will invoke Justice Robertson's "prescription glasses" doctrine from RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087 at paragraph 12), demonstrating that the legal threshold is a question of law for the Court and that Laurentian's contemporaneous repeatability logs irrefutably establish a systematic investigation.
Case Study 2: Advanced Industrial Manufacturing — Experimental Development of a Multi-Axis Automated Composite Panel Forming and Rapid Curing Line
Scenario & Alignment with RIS-Christie Pitfalls

Borealis Aerospace & Industrial Forming Ltd. ("Borealis"), a mid-sized manufacturer located in Montréal, Québec, designs high-speed automated manufacturing lines for thermo-structural composite panels. During its 2025 taxation year, Borealis undertakes an internal shop-floor experimental development project claiming $1.1 million in SR&ED wages and materials to engineer a continuous induction-heated multi-axis forming press capable of forming and curing 180 geometric variations of structural composite panels within a three-hour cycle time without micro-delamination, resin voids, or thermal warpage.

Over a ten-month period, Borealis's shop-floor engineers and machinists conduct 85 experimental trial runs on an instrumented prototype press line. Whenever warpage or delamination occurs during a run, the lead manufacturing engineer adjusts the induction coil frequency, platen pressure profiles, and cooling rates directly on the machine's programmable logic controller (PLC), overwriting the previous PLC parameter configuration. Although the engineering team achieves a major technological breakthrough—reducing void content below 0.8% and securing patent protection—they maintain no structured written log of the 84 overwritten PLC parameter sets or the quantitative non-destructive ultrasonic test metrics for the scrapped composite panels. Following an on-site review, the CRA RTA disallows the entire claim under subsection 248(1), characterizing the shop-floor work as undocumented "trial-and-error" troubleshooting rather than a systematic investigation adhering to the scientific method, and asserting that the testing lacks documented repeatability as analyzed in RIS-Christie and Kam-Press Metal Products.
Step 1: Project Governance & Shop-Floor SR&ED Segregation

To overcome the CRA's characterization of shop-floor experimentation as routine debugging or unsystematic trial-and-error, Borealis must institute a formal Shop-Floor Experimental Governance Protocol (SFEGP) that structurally separates SR&ED from commercial production. Within Borealis's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Manufacturing Execution System (MES), management must establish a dedicated Experimental Development Cost Centre (900-SRED). Corporate governance rules must prohibit any experimental run from commencing on the shop floor without an approved SR&ED Experimental Test Protocol Ticket signed by the Vice President of Engineering. This ticket explicitly segregates eligible experimental development runs under paragraph 248(1)(c) and commensurate supporting testing under paragraph 248(1)(d) from commercial pilot runs or routine machine calibration, which are statutorily excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i) of the Income Tax Act.

Furthermore, Borealis must establish a bi-weekly SR&ED Technical Review Committee comprising the lead composite materials engineer, the PLC automation architect, and the internal corporate tax manager. The committee's contemporaneous written minutes must formally document the five-stage analytical progression articulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic (at paragraph 16), to which the Federal Court of Appeal referred in RIS-Christie (at paragraph 10): observing the shop-floor failure mode, formulating a clear objective, articulating the underlying thermodynamic or mechanical uncertainty, formulating a specific hypothesis prior to authorizing the next batch of machine trials, and analyzing the resulting experimental data.
Step 2: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation & Automated Repeatability Telemetry

To eliminate the fatal overwrite of test parameters and satisfy the repeatability standard examined in RIS-Christie, Borealis must re-engineer its industrial data capture workflow so that contemporaneous documentation is generated automatically as an intrinsic byproduct of the machine testing itself. Borealis must configure the prototype press line's PLC and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system with an immutable historian database paired with a Git-based version-control repository. Whenever an engineer modifies induction coil frequency, die closure velocity, or thermal ramp rate for an experimental trial, the SCADA historian automatically snapshots the complete parameter array, timestamps the execution window, and assigns a unique, sequential Experiment ID (such as EXP-2025-042).

Each Experiment ID must be linked within a relational engineering database to three mandatory analytical records that establish full third-party repeatability. First, the database must log the specific quantitative hypothesis under test—for example, hypothesizing that stepping the induction coil excitation frequency from 25 kHz to 40 kHz during the resin gelation phase while holding platen consolidation pressure constant at 0.7 MPa will eliminate skin-to-core thermal gradients exceeding 8°C and prevent interlaminar shear failure. Second, the record must attach the raw quantitative measurement outputs from the trial, including ultrasonic C-scan void percentage maps, embedded thermocouple time-series curves, and laser profilometry warpage measurements in µm. Third, the lead engineer must enter a contemporaneous analytical conclusion explaining why the empirical data confirmed or refuted the hypothesis and specifying the exact variable modification required for EXP-2025-043. In addition, Borealis must preserve tagged physical cross-sections of representative failed and successful composite panel coupons cross-referenced to their Experiment IDs for physical inspection by the CRA RTA during the on-site factory tour pursuant to Chapter 5.6.0 of the Claim Review Manual.
Step 3: Contractual & Internal Labour Tracking Restructuring

Even in an in-house manufacturing R&D environment, employment and vendor agreements must be structured to reinforce SR&ED evidentiary compliance under subsection 230(1) of the Income Tax Act. Borealis must update its internal engineering employment contracts and project charters to make the completion of SCADA Experiment ID logs and bi-weekly SR&ED Review Committee minutes a mandatory professional deliverable tied to engineering performance reviews. Time-tracking protocols must require shop-floor engineers and technicians to log hours daily against specific Experiment IDs (EXP-2025-XXX) rather than generic R&D cost codes, ensuring complete auditability of claimed SR&ED wages regarding the nature of the work performed and the specific technological problems addressed.

Where Borealis engages third-party materials testing laboratories in Canada to perform destructive mechanical shear testing or differential scanning calorimetry on composite coupons—expenditures that qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d) as testing commensurate with the needs and directly in support of paragraph 248(1)(c) experimental development—Borealis must restructure its vendor purchase orders. Every subcontracted testing purchase order must mandate that the external laboratory reference Borealis's internal Experiment ID and exact test boundary conditions on the face of the laboratory test certificate and commercial invoice, creating an unbroken documentary chain linking third-party testing expenditures to the systematic investigation.
Step 4: Audit Defense Strategy & Countering RTA "Trial-and-Error" Objections

When the CRA RTA conducts the on-site review and interviews Borealis's shop-floor personnel, Borealis will deploy a two-pronged legal and technical defense rooted directly in RIS-Christie and Northwest Hydraulic. First, by presenting the immutable SCADA/PLC telemetry archives alongside the bi-weekly hypothesis review minutes and tagged physical panel coupons, Borealis provides direct documentary proof that the 85 shop-floor trials were controlled, repeatable experiments in which variables were systematically isolated, measured, and analyzed in accordance with the scientific method, thoroughly refuting any allegation of random "trial-and-error".

Second, recognizing that CRA RTAs are instructed under Chapters 5 and 6 of the Claim Review Manual to record detailed interview notes that are frequently scrutinized by Quality Assurance and the Tax Court of Canada, Borealis will prepare its engineering witnesses prior to the on-site interview to articulate their work clearly through the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. Should any minor documentary gaps exist in early-stage shop-floor records, Borealis will rely on the binding precedent of the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087 at paragraphs 14–16)—subsequently applied by the Tax Court of Canada in decisions such as Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42 at paragraph 118) and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108)—which establishes that while documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between tests is the "sure-fire" evidentiary standard, both documentary and viva voce evidence are admissible, and the court may infer that systematic research was conducted, having regard to the totality of the evidence, where there is a plausible explanation for missing records or where the research is established to have led to a technological advancement.
